A very slow moving warm front stretched from west to east across southern portions of the Quad State the evening of the 20th into the early morning hours of the 21st. Pockets of intermittent dense fog developed, at times accompanied by light rain, and generally with calm or 3mph winds. In Western Kentucky, fog development was most prominent in the Southern Pennyrile and Land Between the Lakes area.

Calm winds and clear skies with low-level saturation behind a cold frontal passage promoted the development of dense fog, mainly over Western Kentucky. Dense fog developed late evening, continuing through the night into the morning hours with clearing latest in the south.
A limited area of dense fog, detected on satellite, developed on the southwest side of a ridge in the Kentucky Pennyrile early morning on the 3rd with clear skies and calm winds.

Following a very dry August, during which most of Western Kentucky receiving an inch of rain or less, Severe Drought (D2) conditions developed in all of Western Kentucky during September. Far southwestern portions of Western Kentucky, from Fulton to Murray, entered Severe Drought early September. Mid-month, Severe Drought expanded across the rest of Western Kentucky. Heavy rainfall from the 19th-24th resulted in significant improvement in drought conditions with Severe Drought only continuing into October for counties near the Tennessee border which generally received near normal September rainfall. Agricultural impacts from the drought occurred heading into harvest season. Burn bans were briefly instituted in many Western Kentucky counties as a result of the drought.

An ice storm occurred along and southeast of a line from Murray to  Madisonville and Owensboro. The thickest glaze of ice was from the Murray area northeast to around Madisonville, where one-third to one-half inch of ice was common.  Numerous power outages occurred in the ice storm area, especially from Murray northeast to Princeton, Madisonville, and Owensboro. At its peak, power outages affected 20,000 customers in western Kentucky. The entire community of Dawson Springs (Hopkins County) was reportedly without power. A few power poles were snapped in Murray. Elsewhere in the ice storm area, icing was mostly one-quarter to one-third inch. A winter storm, with locally major impacts, affected western Kentucky on the 5th with a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain. A brief wintry mix that fell primarily as freezing rain quickly transitioned to plain rain later that morning and afternoon across much of the region. Peak accumulations ranged from a trace to a half inch of snow and sleet along with a glaze of ice. Further north along and north of Interstate 69, more snow and sleet had occurred on the onset before transitioning to a prolonged period of freezing rain and eventually plain rain. Wrap around moisture caused one final burst of snow into the morning hours on the 6th after a lull that evening with patchy freezing drizzle. A strong storm system led to significant impacts. Heavy rainfall amounts of 3 to 4.5 inches produced areas of flash flooding, with numerous road closures. The heavy rain drove the Ohio River above flood stage at Uniontown. Very strong wind gusts occurred, ranging between 50 and about 70 mph. These were associated with both thunderstorms and gradient winds afterwards. The line of storms moved through during the late morning and early afternoon, and then very strong gradient winds continued for several hours afterwards through the afternoon. An indirect fatality occurred the following day during cleanup operations. A 69-year-old man in Calloway County was killed when a large branch landed on him while he was cutting up the tree. The magnitude and duration of this wind produced significant damage to trees, power lines, and other outdoor property such as fences. Soggy ground due to the exces

A surface low pressure center tracked northeast through southeast Missouri into central Illinois during the afternoon and evening. The track of the low resulted in increasing low level winds in western Kentucky in the evening. West to southwest winds gusted to between 40 and 50 mph at times. The peak wind gust in western Kentucky was measured at 48 mph at the mesonet site near Marion.

Strong gusty west to southwest winds occurred in the wake of a cold front that arced southeast from a low pressure center over central Illinois. Peak measured wind gusts were near 40 mph along and south of a line from Paducah to Madisonville. The highest measured gusts were 40 mph at Paducah and 41 mph at Fort Campbell/Hopkinsville.

Strong southwest winds ahead of a cold front gusted from 40 to 46 mph across western Kentucky during the pre-dawn hours of the 17th. Behind the cold front, another surge of strong northwest winds in the evening gusted from 40 to 45 mph. The peak wind gusts during the early morning hours were 46 mph at Cadiz, 43 mph at Marion and Central City, 41 mph at Mayfield, Elkton, Calhoun, Murray, and Hopkinsville, and 40 mph at Paducah. The peak gust in the evening was 43 mph at Paducah and 41 mph at Owensboro.

Owner describes seeing strong straight-line winds heading towards his house from west to east. When the winds hit the house, they knocked out one of the chimneys and roof apex on the west facing side of the house, causing a large amount of damage both outside and inside of the historic home. In addition to the house, winds destroyed a barn located to the south of the house, along with several sheds. When winds hit the older house, sitting to the west, it lifted off the roof structure and threw it to the ESE, hitting the roof and chimney of the new house. This caused the chimney to collapse and fall, leading to significant damage to the side of the house and porches. Thankfully no one was injured in this incident. In addition, several other nearby outbuildings sustained damage, as did the siding on the houses, but all other structures on the property were fine.

All damage was laying uniformly towards the ENE.

Numerous trees were observed to be uprooted and snapped along Minerva Tuckahoe Road, consistent with EF1 intensity. Additionally, a  structure was damaged on T Wenz Road, which confirmed the estimated EF1 intensity, with considerable roof coverage loss and a partial collapse of the second story brick wall. Due to a lack of access along the rest of T Wenz Road and Lee Creek, it is unknown how many trees and builders were damaged. The last known sign of damage, a few trees uprooted, was observed along Tuckahoe Road. It is believed the tornado dissipated before the Ohio River.

Following a very dry August, during which most of Western Kentucky receiving an inch of rain or less, Severe Drought (D2) conditions developed in all of Western Kentucky during September. Far southwestern portions of Western Kentucky, from Fulton to Murray, entered Severe Drought early September. Mid-month, Severe Drought expanded across the rest of Western Kentucky. Heavy rainfall from the 19th-24th resulted in significant improvement in drought conditions with Severe Drought only continuing into October for counties near the Tennessee border which generally received near normal September rainfall. Agricultural impacts from the drought occurred heading into harvest season. Burn bans were briefly instituted in many Western Kentucky counties as a result of the drought.

Broad high pressure over the middle Mississippi River Valley resulted in temperatures surging to the mid-to-upper 90s with dew points in the mid 70s, yielding heat indices around 105-110 mainly from the 16th-19th in Western Kentucky with some locally higher values, mainly in the Jackson Purchase Area. Some sites reached heat indices high enough for duration based heat criteria starting on the 14th-15th, mainly near the Tennessee border. Northwest Kentucky had more frequent dew points in the lower 70s, limiting heat advisory criteria duration. A cold front the night of the 19th-20th brought an end to the heat. The highest observed heat index was 115 on the 19th at the McLean County Kentucky Mesonet site.

As the system's north to south oriented cold front moved east through the Lower Ohio Valley on the 15th, several storms produced widespread hail across north central Kentucky. recent.narrative: Snow fell across Martin County on January 19th, with accumulations increasing throughout the day. An early public report at 1100EST noted an estimated 1.0 inch of snow at Tomahawk. By evening, at 1715EST, the Department of Highways reported a measured 3.0 inches at their maintenance garage near Inez. The final storm total of a measured 4.0 inches was reported by the CO-OP observer (Inez 2E) at 800EST on January 20th.

Snow began falling in Martin County on the afternoon of January 10th and continued in some areas until after midnight. The following morning, on January 11th, storm total reports indicated a north-to-south increase in snowfall amounts. Reports from the northern part of the county included 2.3 inches of measured new snow from the CO-OP Observer (Inez 2E) and approximately 3.0 inches from the Highway Department 1 mile west-northwest of Inez. A higher total was reported in the southern part of the county, where the Highway Department noted approximately 4.0 inches of snow along KY-292.

A mix of snow and freezing rain impacted Martin County on January 5th and 6th. Snowfall accumulations of at least a couple of inches were widespread, though no reports exceeded 4 inches. A public report from near Milo showed an accumulation of approximately 0.25 inches of ice.

The AWOS station at the Big Sandy Airport reported a peak wind gust of only 36 mph at 1135 AM EST. However, Martin County dispatch reported that there were instances of trees and powerlines blown down across all of the county.

A cooperative observer 2 miles E of Inez reported a storm total snowfall of 6.4 inches at 7:00am on January 16 (this is an increase from 2.5 inches measured the morning before around the same time). Inez proper also reported 7.0 inches at 10am on January 16.
The large storm in Pike County led to an outflow boundary which moved through Martin County, causing a tree to blown down near Jack's Branch and KY-292.

Historic flash flooding struck parts of far western Kentucky. Among the hardest hit counties was Graves County, which had not completely recovered from a catastrophic tornado in December of 2021. The city of Mayfield, which bore the brunt of the December 2021 tornado, experienced catastrophic flooding that inundated dozens of homes, businesses, schools, and various other institutions. The governor of Kentucky visited the city of Mayfield to tour the damage. Some smaller communities suffered catastrophic damage, such as Arlington in Carlisle County, where multiple homes were flooded. Swiftly moving water through Arlington prompted water rescues from emergency services. Widespread flash flooding of roads made travel difficult or impossible for several hours during the peak of the heaviest rainfall in the morning. Among the most impactful road closures was Interstate 69 in southwest Graves

costliest.narrative: An EF2 tornado touched down along County Highway 164 just north of I-24 and caused some shingle damage to a house and pretty significant damage to a couple of barns. It continued east uprooting or snapping dozens of trees along its path. Many homes experienced mainly roof damage along River Bend Road and Westminster Place. The tornado crossed Hwy-41A and snapped about a half dozen power poles. Some damage to a house and outbuildings occurred along Harry Berry Lane before the tornado lifted just east of County Highway 109. Estimated peak winds with this tornado were 118 mph. The tornado occurred within a broader area of sporadic straight line winds that swept across southern Christian County.

The tornado formed on the south side of downtown Hopkinsville and moved east, lifting on the northeast side of the interchange of U.S. 41 and U.S. 68. A number of structures were damaged in this highly populated urban area. Major roof damage occurred at a brick church, with part of the roof and decking removed. Many trees were uprooted and several were snapped. The roof and a small part of a wall were removed on a brick home. Several businesses sustained minor to moderate roof damage, and a few sustained major damage. A gas station canopy was destroyed, along with gas pumps. A few businesses sustained damage to doors and windows. Peak winds were estimated near 115 mph at the church (DI 17, DOD 5).

A National Weather Service damage survey revealed straight-line winds caused extensive damage in parts of Hopkinsville. Scattered large tree branches were down, and several shallow-rooted trees were uprooted. Two 2-story buildings downtown had windows blown out, and the outer walls collapsed. Several trees fell on homes, causing major damage. Minor damage to homes included siding, shingle, and gutter damage. Winds were estimated from 80 to 85 mph in most places, with isolated spots reaching 90 mph.

A minivan became disabled in floodwaters on East 9th Street near the railroad tracks in Hopkinsville. Highway 41 was closed and impassable south of Hopkinsville. An approximate estimate of road closures countywide was about 25. Only three roads were damaged, and they were repaired rather quickly with gravel. There were three homes flooded. Around a dozen or so homes were affected with water in carports, basements, and crawl spaces.

An EF-2 tornado began in Trigg County, southeast of Cadiz, crossing over into Christian County at Newstead Rd. The tornado tracked eastward, shifting to east-northeastward near I-24. After crossing the Pennyrile Parkway and Fort Campbell Blvd, the tornado lifted at John Rivers Rd northwest of Pembroke. Damage to numerous homes occurred due to downed trees. Two homes were directly impacted due to the tornado winds, with roof damage. Many trees were snapped or uprooted. Several farm buildings were damaged. Peak estimated winds with this tornado in Christian County, and for the tornado as a whole, were 115 mph.
A wind gust to 67 mph was measured at the mesonet site six miles north of Hopkinsville. Four miles west-northwest of town, shingles and siding were blown off houses and trees were down.

costliest.narrative: Historic flash flooding struck parts of far western Kentucky. Among the hardest hit counties was Graves County, which had not completely recovered from a catastrophic tornado in December of 2021. The city of Mayfield, which bore the brunt of the December 2021 tornado, experienced catastrophic flooding that inundated dozens of homes, businesses, schools, and various other institutions. The governor of Kentucky visited the city of Mayfield to tour the damage. Some smaller communities suffered catastrophic damage, such as Arlington in Carlisle County, where multiple homes were flooded. Swiftly moving water through Arlington prompted water rescues from emergency services. Widespread flash flooding of roads made travel difficult or impossible for several hours during the peak of the heaviest rainfall in the morning. Among the most impactful road closures was Interstate 69 in southwest Graves

Widespread major damage to trees and power lines was reported in a path across southern Graves County. The area from Wingo to Sedalia was in the most concentrated damage path. Trees were down across numerous roads. Power poles were snapped in the Wingo area. A garage was blown off its foundation near Wingo. A jeep was moved about 40 feet and pushed into a fence. Shingles were blown off houses. Trees landed on houses and vehicles. An empty school bus was demolished. About 1,000 utility customers were still without power the following morning, mostly in the Wingo area.

Several farm buildings, including a large shop, lost parts or all of their roofs, with several smaller structures destroyed. At least a couple of homes had mainly minor damage to roofs or siding. Dozens of large trees were snapped or uprooted. The tornado travelled right along Highway 94 from southwest of Cuba to the Lynnville area. Peak winds were estimated near 95 mph.

After the tornado lifted, straight-line winds broadened and moved through the south side of Mayfield. The storm survey focused on Macedonia St where multiple large trees were uprooted or snapped, with one tree falling onto a house. Additional tree damage was reported on Backusberg Rd, Tom Dr, and near KY-940. Nearly half of Graves County was without power mid-morning.

A few billboards were damaged. Several metal barns lost roofing. Wooden power poles were leaning. A carport was flipped. A few trees and large branches were blown down. Peak winds were estimated near 90 mph.

costliest.narrative: An EF-2 tornado began at 11:08 AM CST just west of the intersection of Old Mayfield Road and McNeil Road. Traveling north-northeast, the tornado paralleled Old Mayfield Road, doing significant roof, siding, and fascia damage to numerous homes and a few businesses. A few homes had most of their roofing structures completely removed. Several outbuildings were completely destroyed. County emergency management officials assessed the damage and found four homes were destroyed and 68 homes were damaged. Numerous wooden power poles were snapped or tilted by tornadic winds. After crossing Hardmoney Road, the tornado did damage to homes, trees, and outbuildings along Michael Drive West before dissipating around 11:10 AM CST. There was enough hail to cause a vehicle accident near exit 16. Small drifts of hail were still visible along the interstate into the early afternoon hours.

Historic flash flooding struck parts of far western Kentucky. Among the hardest hit counties was Graves County, which had not completely recovered from a catastrophic tornado in December of 2021. The city of Mayfield, which bore the brunt of the December 2021 tornado, experienced catastrophic flooding that inundated dozens of homes, businesses, schools, and various other institutions. The governor of Kentucky visited the city of Mayfield to tour the damage. Some smaller communities suffered catastrophic damage, such as Arlington in Carlisle County, where multiple homes were flooded. Swiftly moving water through Arlington prompted water rescues from emergency services. Widespread flash flooding of roads made travel difficult or impossible for several hours during the peak of the heaviest rainfall in the morning. Among the most impactful road closures was Interstate 69 in southwest Graves

Numerous trees and large branches were broken near the parkway. The tornado continued as far as the southwest city limit of Central City. Near the southwest city limit, a metal commercial structure suffered extensive roof loss and some damage to walls. Nearby, a house roof was damaged and windows were blown out. A nearby church received minor structural damage. A road sign along the Western Kentucky Parkway was blown about a tenth of a mile. Estimated peak wind speeds were near 95 mph.

Several roads were flooded, including a few main roads. Several water rescues were conducted. Water was close to four feet deep over Kentucky 181 near Highway 601, where at least one car stalled out. costliest.narrative: The Little Sandy River at Grayson rose above its 21 foot flood stage on the last day of February. On March 1st the river crested at 27.95 feet, tentatively the fifth highest crest of all time at this location, then returned to its banks the next day on the 2nd. Extensive property damage occurred in the town of Grayson while the river was out of its banks and backwater along streams and creeks drained into the Little Sandy. Many of the local roadways became unusable as flood water spilled into the town and up toward the I-64 corridor.

recent.narrative: In the wake of a cold front early in the morning on December 29th, strengthening wind gusts took shape across northeast Kentucky for most of the day. The strongest gust of note from that day was recorded at the Emergency Operations Center in Boyd County of 48 miles per hour shortly after midnight, and remained elevated through the morning and afternoon. Tens to thousands of homes lost power in the midst of the elevated winds due to downed trees and power lines that occurred across the area. The pressure gradient eased its grip over the area by that evening as high pressure began to build into the Tennessee Valley.

A late night cold frontal passage quickly dashed through northeast Kentucky around midnight on December 19th and caused significant damage to parts of the Central Appalachians. Behind the front, strong winds aloft continued to mix down to the surface and cause occasional breezy to strong gusts at the surface. A 43 mile per hour wind gust was recorded at the Boyd County Emergency Operations Center around sunrise that morning. A few thousand customers were without power as a result of downed trees and power lines caused by the strong front. Winds subsided by the middle of the morning as high pressure began to build into the western Ohio Valley.

A clipper system progressing over the area from December 13th to the 14th contributed to the most notable snow accumulations in northeast Kentucky for the month. The orientation of these snow showers from southeast to northwest caused a staggered start time to precipitation, first falling over Greenup County around midday and slowly reaching southward into Lawrence County by that evening. ||Heavy snow showers swept through the region late on the 13th into the early morning on the 14th, before the disturbance shifted eastward out of the area. While northeast Kentucky remained mostly south of the heaviest snow from this event, accumulations still ranged between 1 to 4 inches for Boyd, Carter, Greenup, and Lawrence Counties.

During the predawn hours of December 8th, snow showers began to spread across northeast Kentucky due to a passing disturbance. Local cooperative observers measured snow amounts of less than an inch with their morning observation, followed by amounts nearing 2 to 4 inches later that afternoon and evening when a heavier band of snow laid over the area. This winter storm quickly pressed eastward that evening, allowing for high pressure to build in from the west and for drier weather to filter back into the area.

Snow showers spread into northeast Kentucky shortly after midnight on December 2nd as a low pressure system swept through the region. This set forth a period of snow showers into the late morning hours before quickly dashing to the east by midday. Precipitation fell as predominantly snow in Kentucky where sub-freezing temperatures prevailed, resulting in snow amounts between 1 to 2 inches, measured by local cooperative observers and CoCoRaHS volunteers.

Snowfall totals with this quick event ranged from half an inch to an inch across northeast Kentucky.

The front arrived into eastern Kentucky around midnight and swept through the area during the early morning on the 5th. Gusts of 35 to 45 miles per hour were common around the state during that time as the front continued its passage overhead. Downed trees and power lines resulted in thousands of power outages to customers within eastern Kentucky. Winds subsided quickly after sunrise on the 5th as high pressure built into the Tennessee Valley.

Breezy to strong wind gusts became common across northeast Kentucky on the afternoon of January 12th in the midst of a passing low pressure system. Gusts on the order of 30 to 35 miles per hour were noted that afternoon and evening, which resulted in a few areas of tree damage and power outages. Winds began to ease off on the morning of January 13th once the low level jet associated with the system migrated to the northeast.

During the late evening hours of December 4th, a cold front progressed through the Ohio Valley and promoted strong to gusty winds in its wake. The front arrived into eastern Kentucky around midnight and swept through the area during the early morning on the 5th. The strongest wind gust for the area was measured in Boyd County, where a Mesonet station observed a 49 mile per hour gust near the town of Ashland. Gusts of 35 to 45 miles per hour were common around the state during that time as the front continued its passage overhead. Downed trees and power lines resulted in thousands of power outages to customers within eastern Kentucky. Winds subsided quickly after sunrise on the 5th as high pressure built into the Tennessee Valley.

While some isolated wind gusts accompanied late morning strong thunderstorms with a cold front, gusts picked up in earnest later that afternoon and evening as the jet winds aloft were able to mix down to the surface. In Kentucky, the strongest wind observation occurred at Mesonet station in Boyd County of 55 miles per hour on the evening of the 29th. Generally around the area, gusts up to 40 to 45 miles per hour were common in the wake of the frontal passage, contributing to widespread power outages late that afternoon into the evening hours. While still breezy overnight, the low level jet shifted northward, eliminating the stronger wind gusts heading into December 30th.

Tens to thousands of homes lost power in the midst of the elevated winds due to downed trees and power lines that occurred across the area. The pressure gradient eased its grip over the area by that evening as high pressure began to build into the Tennessee Valley.

A 43 mile per hour wind gust was recorded at the Boyd County Emergency Operations Center around sunrise that morning. A few thousand customers were without power as a result of downed trees and power lines caused by the strong front. Winds subsided by the middle of the morning as high pressure began to build into the western Ohio Valley.

costliest.narrative: Multiple trees were snapped. Many tree branches and some trees fell on multiple homes, which inflicted damage. At one point there were 65 trees covering main and secondary roads across the county. All main roads were back open on the afternoon of the 4th, and crews then focused on secondary roads. Many roads were closed as cleanup continued. Emergency management reported 28 residential structures had some form of damage, and a dozen commercial structures were damaged as well. These included farming structures and equipment. One family was displaced from their mobile home because of damage from a fallen tree. A county state of emergency was declared. Peak winds were estimated near 105 mph.

Historic flash flooding struck parts of far western Kentucky. Among the hardest hit counties was Graves County, which had not completely recovered from a catastrophic tornado in December of 2021. The city of Mayfield, which bore the brunt of the December 2021 tornado, experienced catastrophic flooding that inundated dozens of homes, businesses, schools, and various other institutions. The governor of Kentucky visited the city of Mayfield to tour the damage. Some smaller communities suffered catastrophic damage, such as Arlington in Carlisle County, where multiple homes were flooded. Swiftly moving water through Arlington prompted water rescues from emergency services. Widespread flash flooding of roads made travel difficult or impossible for several hours during the peak of the heaviest rainfall in the morning. Among the most impactful road closures was Interstate 69 in southwest Graves

Twelve structures were damaged, including a poultry barn that was a total loss. Most of the structures were homes with roof damage. Scattered trees and power lines were down.

This EF-1 tornado began with a cluster of damage along Kentucky 307 just south of Johnson Rd, including on Bizzle Road and Laine Road. Around two dozen trees were blown down, and a grain bin was destroyed on Laine Road. This was the strongest and widest portion of the tornado track. The tornado proceeded northeastward, with damage to a portion of a tree line south of Johnson Road. Large branches and smaller limbs were found on Rushton Road and Kentucky 1529. A tree fell on a house along Highway 1529. A large section of a tree fell onto a home on Wilson Road. The tornado appeared to have lifted shortly after crossing Wilson Road. Peak winds were estimated near 105 mph.
Several farm outbuildings sustained partial or complete loss of metal roofing. A carport was damaged. Some trees were down. Peak winds were estimated around 80 mph.

A narrow EF-1 tornado (peak winds of 100mph) began on KY-94 just east of Hickman. The tornado then slowly moved southeast, mostly across open fields, doing sporadic minor tree damage before snapping 3 power poles along and near KY-166. The tornado ended near Rice Lane south of KY-166. Photos from the event show a very narrow funnel consistent with the narrow damage path.

A large tree limb was downed by thunderstorm winds near the intersection of KY-94 and KY-1212. Further south, a 46mph wind gust was measured at KY-1128 and Alexander Rd where a basketball goal with a water base was blown backwards.
A center pivot turned over on Sycamore Rd and a tree was blown down onto a house in Hickman as a surging portion of a thunderstorm line progressed eastward through northwestern Fulton County.
A cold air funnel formed near Hickman.

Late February flooding continued into early March along the Mississippi River at Hickman. Minor flooding of low-lying areas occurred. River levels fell just below flood stage by the early afternoon on the 1st.

costliest.narrative: Widespread flash flooding occurring in Hickman. Numerous roads were closed or impassable. Five homes in Hickman were evacuated due to flash flooding. Numerous streets remained closed through the morning. An area along Kentucky 94 in the downtown Hickman area was blocked for several days where a mudslide occurred, taking trees with it. Kentucky 125 was blocked near the Hickman city limits. The Fulton County mesonet site located two miles east of Hickman observed 11.28 of rain in 33 hours from 3 AM August 3rd through 12 noon August 4th. This broke the previous 2-day rainfall record for Fulton County, which was 9.80 back on January 1-2, 1966. The 24-hour record also was shattered, with 9.69 occurring between 8 AM August 3rd and 8 AM August 4th. The previous 24-hour record for the county was 7.24 set back on September 23, 2006.

This EF-1 tornado began near the center of Hickman, in the Terrace Drive and Sunset Street area. Damage to trees and power lines occurred in this neighborhood. This tornado tracked to the east-southeast, with more tree damage on Bayou Street and Johnson Lane. A large tree fell onto a home on Myron Cory Drive. The tornado crossed Kentucky 125 and proceeded to 7th Street, where the most significant cluster of damage occurred with several trees uprooted, portions of a few trees snapped, and power line damage. One of the trees fell onto a car. The storm was at its peak width around Kentucky 125 and 7th Street. Additional damage to trees occurred on Nelson Street and Harrison Street. The damage path ended at this point, with the tornado lifting after moving into open areas east of Nelson Street. Peak winds were estimated near 105 mph.

This weak tornado touched down in agricultural fields south of Highway 1128. As it moved north along Highway 1127, it damaged hog barns, mainly removing roofs. The tornado dissipated in a field just east of Highway 1127. A couple of trees were uprooted. Peak winds were estimated near 75 mph.

While the bulk of strong winds with storms stayed east of Kentucky, there was one instance of quarter size hail observed by a member of the public in Lawrence County. Storms continued to travel southeastward out of the area through the evening as the front pivoted overhead.

The tornado then tracked eastward, skipping along an almost six and a half mile track, crossing US 23 and the Big Sandy River just north of Louisa before continuing into West Virginia. A roughly 400 yard wide swath of rather extensive tree damage occurred on the west side of the Big Sandy River near a logging yard and two semi trailers were overturned at that location.
Significant flooding was observed along Kentucky Route 3 with water beginning to flow into adjacent homes. The Fallsburg campground was almost completely underwater.
Nats Creek Road was impassable in several spots due to high water. Water also damaged portions of Copper Road.
Multiple trees were blown down on Route 3 in the Fallsburg area.
A downed tree along US Route 23 caused power outages in the area of Louisa.

While the creek was out of its banks, portions of the Blaine Elementary School, low sections of Route 32, Blaine Community Park, and agricultural fields adjacent to the creek were all flooded.

The side and top of a barn was blown off along KY-1722 near the Licking River. Most of the debris was blown eastward across the road and into the trees across the street. In addition, numerous trees behind the barn and along the river received broken limbs as the wind came through.

The garage door had been removed at time of survey. Meanwhile, the house next door (north of above-mentioned house/west side of the street) received siding damage to the south-facing side of the house, and had it's AC unit flipped over on the same side. The house across the street also sustained a broken window, and missing shingles/flashing.

A well constructed barn was destroyed by what was determined to be straight line wind damage just north of the community of Haldeman. The barn was on a knob and in an exposed location. The roof was blown off, and the sides then collapsed.

A large pine tree was uprooted in front of a house on Bluebank Road, just north of the intersection with Ramey Ridge Road. The tree fell southward, hitting the front porch of the house. The extent of the damage is unknown.

The most severe damage occurred in downtown Princeton, where a business lost its roof and several homes suffered minor to major damage due to trees falling onto homes.  Numerous large tree limbs were downed across the city. Emergency management also reported power poles snapped, a tree fell onto a house on U.S. 62 on the west side of Princeton, while another tree falling onto a house on W Green St, destroying it.

Portions of several state highways were closed, including Highway 139 south of Farmersville, Highway 91 northwest of White Sulphur, Highway 293 southwest of Princeton, and Highway 126 from Highway 128 to the Trigg County line. The bulk of the flooding ended on the 16th, but the time was extended into the 17th for a fatality that occurred when flood waters washed a man's car off the levee and into the spillway of Lake Beshear.
Flash flooding along Goose Creek closed Highway 128 southeast of Princeton.

Emergency management also reported power poles snapped, a tree fell onto a house on U.S. 62 on the west side of Princeton, while another tree falling onto a house on W Green St, destroying it.

An EF-3 tornado (max of EF-2 in Caldwell County) began northeast of Eddyville in Lyon County before crossing into Caldwell County near Pleasant Valley Rd. The tornado tracked east-northeastward through the entirety of Caldwell County, crossing over into Hopkins County north of I-69 and south of Young Cemetery Rd. The tornado briefly weakened northwest of Princeton. It then strengthened producing EF-2 damage north of Princeton near KY-293 N, blowing apart a manufactured home. Additional structures, trees, and power lines were damaged in Caldwell County. For Caldwell County, 4 people were injured and one person (54m, indirect) suffered a heart attack while cleaning up debris the following day, passing away as a result. Peak estimated winds with the Caldwell County portion of the tornado were 130 mph.

Peak winds were estimated near 100 mph. A mobile home was lifted and moved about 30 feet. The mobile home as well as a small barn were destroyed. Several trees were snapped, with large limbs down as well. The brief tornado occurred along Highway 139, just northeast of the Interstate 24 exit.
Trees were downed in Princeton as a thunderstorm line moved eastward through Caldwell County. Most of Caldwell County lost power as a result of morning thunderstorms.

A woman was rescued from flash flooding near Farmersville. Deputy sheriffs responded to a county road just northwest of Farmersville, where a woman was trapped in a vehicle that had been swept off the road and wedged between two trees. The Jeep was almost completely submerged. A law officer attached a tow strap to himself and waded about 40 feet into the water, then broke a window to help the woman out of the vehicle. The deputy attached the tow strap to her, and another deputy helped pull them to safety.

A wind gust to 58 mph was recorded at the Kentucky mesonet site near Princeton. There were multiple reports of trees down in Princeton. Trees were down over Highway 903 four miles south-southwest of Princeton.

recent.narrative: Torrential rainfall during the morning resulted in flooding of roads in Henderson County including part of Hwy 41. Over 4.5in of rainfall were observed in multiple locations: 4.74in at Robards, 4.71in at Coryden, and 4.52in at Henderson.
Heavy rainfall resulted in ditches overflowing north of Henderson. A driveway was flooded with half a foot of water. Peak hourly rainfall rates reached approximately 1-1.5.
Flash flooding was observed on US-60 at 4th St and 12th St with traffic rerouted. Rainfall rates in the area were estimated by radar at around an inch over 45 minutes.
Power lines were downed by thunderstorm winds onto S. Green St. Further north, a 50mph gust was recorded near the intersection of US-60 and US-41.

Torrential rainfall rates of 1.5'' in an hour resulted in flash flooding in Henderson. Numerous vehicles were stuck in floodwaters including on North Green St and Ingram St, between 7th and 1st Street. Portions of Alvesia St were also closed due to floodwaters.
Hail measured to penny size was reported south of Henderson via mPING.

costliest.narrative: Torrential rainfall rates of 1.5'' in an hour resulted in flash flooding in Henderson. Numerous vehicles were stuck in floodwaters including on North Green St and Ingram St, between 7th and 1st Street. Portions of Alvesia St were also closed due to floodwaters.
A microburst occurred on U.S. Highway 41 in the Robards area, then spread westward a short distance on Highway 416. Three trees were down on houses, and one tree was down on a car.

An EF-1 tornado passed just to the west of the Smith Mills community in Henderson County. The tornado developed along JJ Utley Road. Traveling north-northeast along Greenlick Baptist Church Road, the tornado destroyed a farm outbuilding. The tornado crossed Kentucky Highway 359 just south of Smith Mills where several trees suffered extensive large limb damage. Continuing north-northeast, the tornado passed through a cemetery along Grandpa Jones Road where several large trees were snapped. The tornado diminished as it reached Kentucky Highway 136 just west of Smith Mills. Peak winds were estimated near 95 mph.
A house suffered major roof shingle loss on Highway 351 just east of Zion. Further down the road on route 351, a large barn lost part of its roof.
Trees were blown down in the vicinity of U.S. Highway 60 near Baskett, Spottsville, and Reed.
Several trees and power lines were down in eastern Henderson County.

recent.narrative: A picture on social media showed downed trees and power lines blocking Croley Bend Road in Williamsburg.
Trees and powerlines were reported to have been blown down in the Bearkat Drive vicinity in Williamsburg.
The 911 call center reported trees down on Keswick Road in southern Whitley County.
Trees were reported to have been blown down on Lick Fork Road in eastern Whitely County.
Trees were reported to have been blown down in the Mountain Ash community.
Trees were reported to have been blown down on US-25W near the intersection with Lick Fork Road.

costliest.narrative: The NWS Survey team determined that damage incurred near the community of Deering was consistent with straight line winds, with maximum wind gusts estimated to be between 80 and 90 mph. The most significant damage occurred to a barn just off Akins Lane, about 7 miles SW of Corbin - in which the barn was destroyed. There were numerous trees uprooted between Frankfort School Road and Bee Creek Road, and from there to Linda Lane, just off Casey Road. Several homes sustained damage from trees that fell on roofs. Of notable interest were eyewitness reports of a circulation that tracked across a small pond in one of the residential areas. Based on the description of the circulation not being in contact with the cloud base, and the location of this event over a pond approximately 300 years off the flanking (west) side of the core of the most destructive winds, the NWS believes this may have bee

Widespread wind damage occurred in the Woodbine community, with many trees uprooted and snapped - specifically along Perkins Street. One mobile home suffered significant damage when a large tree fell onto it.
The survey team surveyed a RV park along Rosetown Church Road near the community of Youngs Creek. The park had multiple trees uprooted, and RVs that were toppled and/or destroyed.
A large tree fell onto a roof of a house located on Akins Lane near the intersection with Bee Creek Road. Several trees of various sizes in adjacent yards were uprooted as well.
A tree was blown down onto a house along Corinth Cemetery Road.
A tree was blown down onto a house along Corinth Cemetery Road.

recent.narrative: Report of hail measured to penny size was submitted via mPING. Time was estimated by radar.
Numerous photos of a cold air funnel that developed in a nearly stationary cell by Knottsville were taken by the public and relayed by broadcast media.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous trees and power lines on the east side of Owensboro and to the east of town as well.
Heavy rainfall northeast of Owensboro resulted in the closure of KY-1831 due to flooding as radar estimated rainfall peaked at 2 in an hour.
Straight-line winds from a storm moving through Owensboro brought down a large portion of an awning over a shopping center, which fell onto several parked vehicles.
Penny size hail was measured near Stanley.

costliest.narrative: A severe storm produced a swath of hail up to the size of baseballs and wind gusts up to 50 mph from near St Joseph through the south and east sides of Owensboro. The area of Cummins Road just south of St Joseph sustained the most significant damage. Several homes sustained broken siding and windows, as well as roof damage. The storm continued to damage roofs and break windows as it passed near Panther Creek Park and through the south and east sides of Owensboro. Scores of vehicles sustained damage.
Widespread straight-line wind damage occurred in northern Daviess County through the city of Owensboro with several homes damaged, at least a couple dozen trees down, and power poles snapped.

Trees were down in Owensboro. Three miles west of Owensboro, a mobile home was lifted and moved about 4 to 5 feet. A nearby carport was moved into a neighbor's yard. Several barns were destroyed in the area.

Pockets of wind damage occurred in western Daviess County. Two garages collapsed west of Highway 81, a few miles north-northwest of Moseleyville. In and near the small community of Rome, there was considerable wind damage. A pole barn was blown down. A semi was blown off the road on Highway 81. A power line was down. A large pine tree and a weeping willow tree were blown down. A wind gust to 61 mph was measured at the Owensboro airport before the power went out to the system.

An EF-0 tornado touched down 2 miles northwest of St. Joseph in western Daviess County, traveled eastward 2.66 miles, and lifted 1 mile northeast of St. Joseph. Numerous large tree limbs were downed along the damage path. A few hog barns suffered roof damage. One house had a small area of shingles removed. The estimated peak wind was 80 mph and the maximum path width was 50 yards.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous trees and power lines on the east side of Owensboro and to the east of town as well.

recent.narrative: Flooding was observed in several spots, including at the small tunnel of Caboose Lane and Pond Run Road in Raceland, Red Devil Lane and Diederich Boulevard in Russell, Bellefonte Alley and Ferry Street in Russell, Argillite Road and Turley Avenue in Flatwoods, and near Washington Street and Powell Lane in Flatwoods.
Flooding was observed at the intersection of State Route 207 and Tom Road in Little Sandy.
A tree on school property fell onto the roadway and onto parked vehicles.
In the community of Palmyra, a tree blew down onto Wildcat Lane.
A downed tree blocked portions of State Route 7 in Load.
Water entered first floor apartments on Raceland Avenue. Flooding quickly receded from the building but lingered in the parking lot. A bridge also washed out on County Road.

costliest.narrative: A broken path of damage was noted on the Kentucky side of the tornado track, beginning at the Riverview Cemetery west of Greenup. Additional damage occurred on Seaton Avenue near South 5th Street and in the Greenup Fairgrounds, where a few buildings suffered roof damage and a large tree fell onto another building. The tornado then likely tracked along the Ohio River before intersecting land again on the Kentucky side and causing roof and tree damage to several homes along Calumet Drive.

An EF1 tornado touched down on a hillside south of Little White Oak Road uprooting several trees. The tornado then traveled north across a newly mowed hay field with a convergent pattern evident in the mowed hay, then impacted a house and garage. The tornado tore off a large section of the roof of the home and destroyed the adjacent garage. Residents of the home witnessed the tornado as it was moving across the hay field toward the house and were able to take shelter. The tornado caused additional tree damage as it continued north up a ridge and then onto Cub Run Road.
Multiple areas of downed trees were observed throughout the county.
The scoreboard at Raceland High School was damaged due to strong winds.

Numerous areas of tree and power line damage was observed in the Raceland area. These included Armada Boulevard, Caroline Road, Rams Boulevard, Brown Street, Belmont Road, Meadow Avenue, and Pond Run Road. A few trees fell onto cars and roofs of homes.
In the Crane Creek area, several power lines had fallen due to strong winds.

recent.narrative: An EF-1 tornado (with peak winds of 98mph) began north of Guthrie where several trees were snapped. The narrow tornado moved east across open fields where it flipped a pivot irrigation system. It destroyed a small outbuilding and damaged other smaller buildings nearby. Several power poles were snapped along US-79 and the intersection of US-79 and KY-848.
Max wind gust from Kentucky Mesonet station ZION (5SW Elkton) over the five minute period.
Hail estimated to quarter size was reported in Clifty.
Trees and power lines were downed near Allegre as part of the rear flank downdraft region of a tornado that passed by to the north.

An EF2 tornado started along Shaw Ovil Road in Christian County, continuing east into Todd County, crossing Hwy 189 and eventually lifting to the west of Hwy 181. The worst damage occurred along Blue Hole Road where several chicken houses were completely destroyed and a mobile home was swept away. Dozens of trees were snapped or uprooted and a few outbuildings were damaged. Peak winds for the Todd County portion of the tornado, and the tornado as a whole, were 120mph.
Hail up to the size of quarters fell near the Christian County line just west of Kirkmansville.

This tornado first touched down on Fort Campbell just north of the Sabre Airfield in Montgomery County, TN. The tornado tracked northeastward through northern Clarksville, entering into Todd County 5 miles west of Guthrie. As the tornado continued into southeastern Todd County, sparsely populated areas were affected initially. Hwys 41, 79, and 848 were blocked by debris or power lines and Hwy 181 was blocked by a train due to debris getting caught under the train. Trees were damaged, along with broken glass at a residence on the Dixie-Beeline Highway and destruction of an outbuilding on Old Railroad Lane. Large sections of a roof were removed from a home on Snardon Mill Rd. Much of the damage occurred on the south side of Allensville, where several homes had heavily damaged roofs, along with more trees, power poles, and outbuildings damaged or destroyed. The tornado continued into Logan

Major flash flooding occurred in Todd County. Initially, a small creek along Stokes Chapel Road near Elkton was out of its banks and flooding the road. The flash flooding became more widespread and intense as the day wore on. Evacuations were underway on a few streets in Elkton. North Main Street was closed coming into Elkton. Elk Fork Road was also closed. A total of 15 residences and 3 businesses were impacted in Elkton, mainly on Water Street, North Main, East Main, West Main, and Washington St. About six people were evacuated from three residences on Water Street and East Main Street. At the peak of the flooding, water was over Highways 181 around Elkton and Guthrie, Highway 475, Highway 106, Highway 104 at Old Trenton, Highway 102 near Allensville, and at least ten county roads. A few roads were temporarily closed until they could be repaired.

The long-track tornado that ended in western Todd County transitioned to a damaging wind event near Elkton. On the west side of Elkton, a barn roof was damaged, several house roofs were damaged, and dozens of trees were snapped or uprooted. The most intense damage was observed on the northeast side of Elkton, where steel poles for electrical transmission lines were broken or bent. Peak winds there were estimated near 115 mph. Elsewhere northeast of Elkton, a barn was destroyed. Most of the other damage consisted of roof damage to barns and outbuildings, mostly minor. Numerous trees were blown down.

The tornado tracked from west to east, passing just north of Elkton by only about one mile. Several older barns were damaged or destroyed. Many large trees were uprooted or snapped. Two semi trailers were flipped over. One of the trailers, which was at the intersection of Highways 181 and 106, was storing construction equipment. There was minor roof damage. Peak winds were estimated near 90 mph.

This long-track EF-3 tornado began in western Tennessee near Dyersburg (see Storm Data, Tennessee, Western). It crossed into Todd County from Christian County near the city of Pembroke. The tornado was near the end of its life in Todd County, where it only received a rating of EF-1. In Todd County, dozens of trees were snapped or uprooted. Roofs were blown off several barns. At least one house and several other farm outbuildings sustained minor to moderate roof damage. The windows were blown out of a few structures. The tornado lifted about four miles west of Elkton. This tornado was on the ground for approximately 125 miles across western Tennessee and western Kentucky. The tornado transitioned to a damaging straight-line wind event in the Elkton area.

recent.narrative: The Kentucky Mesonet station 3 miles north of Whitley City reported a peak wind gust of 30 mph at 225 PM EST. However, the Whitley County dispatch reported that multiple trees and a utility line were blown down at both near Whitley City and Pine Knot, suggesting that locally higher wind gusts occurred.

McCreary County had multiple reports of wind damage, all within a fairly short amount of time. At 12:55 PM EDT, a tree was reported to have been blown down on KY-1363 near Yamacraw. At 1:00 PM, another tree was reported to have been blown down at Marshes Siding. Then 5 minutes later, at 1:10 PM, a tree was blown down onto KY-1470 near Strunk. At the same time (1:10 PM) another tree was reported to have blown down in the Hay Creek Community.

The McCreary County Mesonet station, located 3 miles N of Whitley City, only recorded a peak weak gust of 35 mph, which isn't very concerning. However, a picture on social media from a public source showed a large tree was blown down in the Pine Knot Community at 4:40 PM EST, suggesting higher wind gusts in this location.

Sporadic large tree damage was reported across the county. The McCreary County dispatch reported that strong wind gusts had blown down a large tree onto a road around 6:49 PM on the 30th, approximately 3 miles NNW of Hollyhill. At 10:30 PM another large tree was reportedly blocking Lum-Strunk Rd. A third report of a large tree blocking Williamsburg was estimated to have occurred around 3:50 AM on the 31st.
A storm total snowfall of 5.0 inches was reported in Blue Heron at 9am EST.

After a period of mixed precipitation and limited impacts during the morning hours of the 16th, periods of heavy, wet snow fell through the afternoon and evening. The highway department measured a storm total snowfall of 5.0 inches at 2 AM on the 17th. An estimated 4.0 inches was reported in Stearns.

recent.narrative: Snow began falling in Magoffin County on the afternoon of January 10th and continued in some areas until after midnight. The following morning, on January 11th, the CO-OP Observer at the Salyersville Water Works reported a measured storm total snowfall of 4.0 inches.

Two storm total reports came in from Magoffin County, both reading 6.5 inches. The first was made at 8am by the Salyersville Water Works (this is an increase from the 3.0 inches measured the morning before). The community of Hendricks was the second report at 10am (an increase from 4 inches reported the morning before).
A large pine tree was blown down onto KY-1090 (near address 4347 Bear Branch/Stinson Road) around 4:30 PM EDT. The tree took out the powerlines and part of the power pole as well.

The 911 Dispatch reported several instances of downed trees across the county from high winds. ||These reports include:|At 8:15 PM EST - Trees were reported blown down onto Pricy Creek Road, 1 mile S of the community of Cisco. |At 8:20 PM EST - Trees were reported to have been blown down in the Coon Creek community.|At 8:30 PM EST - Trees were reported to have been blown down in the Royalton area.|At 8:35 PM EST - Trees were reported to have been blown down onto the eastward bound lanes of the Mountain Parkway about 1 mile NNW of Ivyton.

The county emergency manager reported that a barn along Improvement Fork Rd. had collapsed due to strong winds, and also that trees had been blown down along Ivy Point Rd. and US-460 at Bear Branch Rd. Local dispatch reported that multiple trees were blown down on US-460, 0.8 miles west of Salyersville, and also directly across KY-7 within the city limits.

Received a report of 3.0 inches (2 SSW of Lakesville) at 3:21am EST and a report of 6.0 inches (Salyersville) at 5:33am EST from the public out of central Magoffin County. A COOP observer at the Salyersville Water Works reported a storm total snowfall of 4.5 inches at 8am EST.

recent.narrative: Heavy snow fell across Owsley County on January 19th and into the 20th. An early measured report of 2.0 inches was received from a county official near Lerose at 1000EST on the 19th. The final storm total was a measured 5.0 inches, reported at 700EST on the 20th by the CoCoRaHS observer located 3.6 miles east-northeast of Booneville.
A storm total of 4.0 inches of measured snow was reported by the CoCoRaHS observer located 3.6 miles east-northeast of Booneville. The measurement was taken at 7:00 AM on January 6th.

Owsley County had the highest total snowfall report out of this event. The observation point 4 ENE of Booneville recorded 9.3 inches of snow as of 7am on January 16. This was an increase from 4.5 inches reported 24 hours before. Also on the 15th, a CoCoRaHS station 2 miles NNW of Lerose reported a similar 4.3 inches of snow had already fallen as of 7:30am.

At 6:45 PM EST, the Kentucky Mesonet site located 2 miles S of Booneville recorded a maximum wind gust of 47 mph. While this isn't High Wind criteria, both Law Enforcement and the Emergency Manager of the county called in additional reports, indicating that wind gusts were higher in these locations. ||These reports include:|At 7:30 PM EST - Local Law Enforcement reported a tree blown down onto KY-11 in Booneville.|At 7:35 PM EST - The Owsley County Deputy Emergency Manager (also a previous NWS Employee) reported that a 3-foot diameter pine tree was blown down at a residence along KY-30E. In addition, 3 hardwood trees were down between Booneville and LeRose.

The local utility company reported that a large tree had been blown down onto and damaged a double circuit adjacent to the substation, located 1/2 miles west of city of Booneville, causing a major power outage across much of the county. Two other power poles, one up the left hand fork of Cow Creek and the other near Vincent, were snapped due to large trees falling onto the power lines. Otherwise, the emergency manager reported a number of small power outages around the county due to fallen trees. The extensive damage required the electric company to call in additional assistance from outside the area.

Two reports were received in the northern part of the county from the public and a CoCoRaHS observer. The public report was made at 10:20am EST, with a storm total snowfall of 6.0 inches. The CoCoRaHS report was made at 7am EST, with a storm total snowfall of 6.7 inches.

recent.narrative: Heavy snow was followed by ice and subsequent damage in Powell County on January 5th and 6th. Heavy snow fell across the county from mid-morning through early afternoon on January 5th. A trained spotter reported a measurement of 2 inches of snow at Waltersville at 1226EST. Shortly after, at 1243EST, an NWS employee measured 3.5 inches of snow 1 mile south-southeast of Stanton. Later in the afternoon, a social media report from Clay City at 1600EST showed about 4.5 inches of snow. The snow then transitioned to freezing rain during the late afternoon and evening hours. Overnight, the combination of snow and ice accumulation led to widespread tree damage. At 0045EST on January 6th, it was reported that at least a half dozen trees were knocked down in Nada. Five minutes later, at 0050EST, a large tree was also reported down on a fence about 1 mile south of Bowen. These specific reports repre

National Weather Service employees reported multiple trees blown down in the county. One of those reports was of a tree uprooted at a residence 1 mile east northeast of Clay City at 1005 AM EST. Another employee reported a tree blown down on a powerline and blocking KY-213 between the General Shale brick plant and Pine View Heights. A tree was also blown down and blocking KY-615 in the vicinity of Courtney Lane. Broadcast media reported that a roof was blown off of a mobile home.

Per Powell County Search and Rescue, a hiker was struck by a falling branch around noon on the Whittleton Branch Campground Hiking Trail, and fell unconcious while pinned beneath the branch. First responders were able to successfully get the hiker out for further treatment. Then at 1:50 PM EDT, public reported a large pine tree blown down onto and blocking Happy Top Road near Clay City.
An NWS Employee reported a medium sized fruit tree having been blown down near the intersection of highways 2026 and 2073 in Stanton at 9:45 PM EST.

Powell County dispatch reported sporadic tree damage across the county. A tree was reportedly blown down onto power lines, taking them down as well, approximately 1 ENE of Stanton at 11:45 PM EST, March 30th. Additional reports of trees blown down onto Thorpe Ridge, Cane Creek, and Black Creek roads were received early on the 31st.

One report was given overnight from a trained spotter that measured 2.8 inches near 3 am EST on the 12th. Storm totals were reported by COOP observers, with 3.3 inches near Stanton at 8am EST, and 5.0 inches further into the western third of the county near Clay City as of 7:00am EST.

recent.narrative: Heavy snow and significant icing impacted Fleming County. On the morning of January 6th, a single observer in Elizaville, reporting for both the CO-OP and CoCoRaHS networks, measured a storm total of 6.1 inches of snow along with 0.30 inches of flat ice accretion at 0700EST. Later that morning at 1107EST, a public report from Flemingsburg showed a measurement of 6.8 inches of combined snow and ice.

One personal weather observing station 2 miles northeast Poplar Plains reported a peak gust of 48 mph at 1114 AM EST. The Fleming-Mason Airport just north of the county reported a peak gusts of 54 mph at 1135 AM EST. Localized damage suggests instances of higher wind gusts. The local COOP observer WRIM2 reported roofing blown off of a nearby residence as well as a blown over carport.

At 1:30 PM EDT, a tree was reported to have been blown down on Foxport Road in Pleasureville. Then at 3:00 PM EDT, another tree was reported down on Ewing Road around 12 highway miles from Flemingsburg.

At 7:15 PM EST, a utility company in Estill County reported two instances of structure damage in the county. The first report was of roofing material having been removed from a barn along KY-170, 1 mile NNE of Flemingsburg. The second was of significant loss of roofing material to a home located near KY-170, 1 mile ENE of the community of Neptune.

A total of 5.7 inches was reported by a CoCoRaHS observer in northwest Fleming County at 7am EST on March 12, while a total of 7.9 inches was reported by a trained spotter near Flemingsburg later in the day at 12:55pm EST.
At 8:25am EST, the Emergency Manager reported greater than 0.25 inches of ice measured at the Fleming County EOC in Flemingsburg.

Late February flooding continued into early March along the Green River at Calhoun. Moderate flooding continued through the early afternoon of the 2nd when the river fell below the moderate flood stage of 26'. Thousands of acres remained underwater in the Calhoun, Rumsey, Island, and Jewel City areas, Minor flooding mainly of bottomland then continued until the morning of the 4th when the river fell just below flood stage.

The flash flooding on the evening of the 15th transitioned to areal flooding early on the 16th. The additional flood waters served to aggravate the ongoing flooding on the Green River through McLean County.
Flash flooding along Yellow Creek, closed a portion of Highway 797 southeast of Beech Grove. One water rescue occurred in this location. Numerous other county roads were flooded across McLean County.

costliest.narrative: River levels rose into flood following a rainy couple weeks in the Green River basin, with a major rainfall event of nearly half a foot of rain on the 15th leading water levels to surge at Calhoun to major flood. Nearly the entire town of Rumsey sustained some amount of water intrusion. Lower Calhoun flooded as well, along with many thousands of acres in the Island and Jewel City areas. Many homes and businesses along the river had flooding issues develop. River levels remained in moderate flood as flooding continued into March.

A very powerful thunderstorm outflow boundary resulted in a mile wide swath of straight line wind damage as the line pushed through Livermore. Several large trees were uprooted with several large tree branches down. A few homes sustained minor shingle damage while a warehouse had partial roof loss. According to Livermore Public Works and McLean County EMA, several power lines were down along with damaged poles in town.

An EF-1 tornado began northwest of Bremen in Muhlenberg County and tracked northeastward into McLean County, continuing through the town of Island before lifting at Doug Hill Rd. The path consisted mostly of tree damage with minor damage to an automotive service building and powerlines in Island. Peak estimated winds with the McLean County portion, and the tornado as a whole, were 90 mph. NWS Paducah thanks NWS Louisville for their assistance surveying this tornado.

Moderate flooding occurred along the Green River. The river crested at 29.69 feet on the Calhoun river gage. This was well above flood stage of 23 feet. This was the highest crest since March 1, 2018, when the river crested at 31.67 feet. Portions of Calhoun and Rumsey were flooded, but few if any residences were evacuated. Thousands of acres were flooded in the Island, Rumsey, and Jewel City areas, but the cropland was mostly dormant. Floodwaters approached Kentucky Highway 81 near the Green River bridge. Some county roads were closed.
A thunderstorm moving northeastward through Livermore caused large trees to be uprooted with a tree falling onto a house.
Small to medium tree limbs were broken.

recent.narrative: Snow fell across Harlan County on January 19th and 20th, with final totals showing a dramatic and clear divide between the lower valleys and the high mountain terrain. Final storm totals from the valley locations were consistently light, with reports coming in on the morning of January 20th. The CO-OP observer 1 miles south of Harlan (HEGK2) measured a total of 2.0 inches at 600EST. An hour later, at 700EST, the Department of Highways reported an estimated 1.5 inches in the city of Harlan. In sharp contrast, snowfall was significantly heavier in the mountains. During the pre-dawn hours of January 20th, at 400EST, the Department of Highways reported an estimated 5.5 inches in the Bledsoe community. At 700EST, they also reported an estimated 4.5 inches on Black Mountain. The highest total for the event was a measured 6.5 inches, reported at 1638EST on the 20th by the CO-OP observer on Pine

Snow fell intermittently in Harlan County, beginning around midday on January 10th and continuing through the evening. On the morning of January 11th, a series of reports from the Department of Highways clearly illustrated a dramatic increase in snowfall totals with elevation. In the lower elevations, a measured 2.5 inches of snowfall was reported in Dayhoit. Higher amounts were found on the mountain passes, with a measured 4.0 inches of new snow reported along US-421 at the Pine Mountain crossing. The highest totals were found at the highest elevations, with approximately 7.0 inches of new snow reported along KY-160 at the Black Mountain crossing.

Snow began in Harlan County on the morning of January 5th, before changing over to freezing rain and rain later in the day. Storm total snowfall measurements taken by CO-OP Observers on the morning of January 6th highlighted the significant impact of elevation on accumulations. At 0751EST, the observer on Pine Mountain (Harlan 3N) reported 4.0 inches of snow. In contrast, the observer at Harlan 1S, located in the valley, reported a lower total of 1.5 inches of snow at 0800EST.

The Harlan County highway department reported approximately 4 inches of snow accumulation along KY-160 near the Virginia-Kentucky state line just below the summit of Big Black Mountain. Elsewhere within the county, reports were generally lower: approximately 2 inches on US-421 atop Pine Mountain and 0.5 to 1.0 inch in the valleys as per a highway department report from Dayhoit and a CoCoRaHS observer report from 5 miles northeast of Baxter.

Two observing stations in Harlan County, one Kentucky Mesonet station atop Big Black Mountains and one AWOS station at the Harlan County Airport, reported peak wind gusts of 45 and 38 mph, respectively. Even so, localized wind damage suggests that there were isolated instances of high gusts. Law enforcement reported multiple instances of trees and power lines blown down in the Cawood, Evarts, and Cumberland areas during the morning hours. In Cawood, one of those trees, a large pine tree, fell onto a mobile home in Cawood, injuring one occupant.

Multiple observations were made across Harlan County on January 16, ranging from 3.5 inches in Harlan proper at 10am, to 7.5 inches in the higher elevations 3 miles N of Harlan at 9:16am. Other reports from the county included 5.4 inches 5 miles NE of Baxter at 7am; 5 inches in the community of Blair at 9:31am; and 4.3 inches 1 mile S of Harlan at 6am.

On the 19th, reports included a measured 2.0 inches from the CO-OP observer at Skyline at 1110EST, and a measured 4.0 inches from the Emergency Manager in Colly by 1607EST. Another measured 2.5 inches was reported by the public near Carcassonne that evening. The highest reported amount for the event was an estimated 5.0 inches, reported by an Emergency Manager near Day at 700EST on the 20th. Other final totals on the morning of the 20th included measured reports of 3.0 inches from the CO-OP observers at both Whitesburg and Skyline.

Snow fell intermittently in Letcher County, beginning around midday on January 10th and continuing through the evening. The following morning, on January 11th, consistent storm total snowfall amounts were reported by CO-OP Observers across the county. Both the observer at Skyline and the observer at Whitesburg 2 SE measured 4.0 inches of new snowfall.

Snow began in Letcher County on the morning of January 5th, before changing over to freezing rain and rain during the afternoon and into the night. Rapid accumulation was reported by the early afternoon. At 1231EST, the public reported 3.5 inches of snow 1 mile south-southwest of Ermine. A report of 3.8 inches was received from near Carcassonne at 1350EST. By the morning of January 6th, final storm totals were being reported. At 0700EST, the CO-OP Observer at station WHBK2 (Whitesburg 2 SE) reported a storm total of 4.0 inches of snow. Around the same time, Letcher County Emergency Management reported approximately 0.1 inches of freezing rain on flat surfaces in Whitesburg. An hour later, at 0800EST, the CO-OP Observer at station SKLK2 (Skyline) reported a measured 4.5 inches of snow.

Two weather observing stations, a personal weather station 1 mile northeast of Payne Gap and a Kentucky Mesonet station 2 miles northwest of Whitesburg, reported wind gusts of 41 mph at 1112 AM EST and 29 mph at 845 AM EST, respectively. Even so, Letcher County dispatch reported that there were multiple trees blown down in the Jenkins, Whitesburg, and Fleming-Neon areas.

While there were no storm total snowfall reports for Letcher County on January 16th, there was a report that verified the Winter Storm Warning the evening before. An amateur radio operator reported 4.5 inches of snow had fallen so far as of 7:53pm January 15 in the community of Blackey.

At 2:55 PM EDT, a public weather station in the Jenkins community measured a wind gust of 58 mph. Only a few minutes later, around 3:00 PM, the Colson Volunteer Fire Department reported that a volunteer firefighter operating the CFD Engine #1 was injured when a tree fell off the side of the hill and struck the vehicle. The firefighter sustained a concussion and abraison to the head and was transported to the hospital for treatment.

The individual who filmed the video was looking east towards KY-90 in Mill Springs, and the rotation moved parallel to KY-90 towards Burnside on radar. Neither Wayne County nor Pulaski County EM reported any damage after investigating the area of interest, and the radar signature was rather weak (maximum VROT signature around 10 knots).
Shortly after 1 PM EST, nickel-sized hail was reported near Cooper.
A tree was blown down onto a mobile home, also causing electrical lines to fall on the home, in the 500 block of South Main Street in Monticello.

recent.narrative: Snow fell intermittently in Laurel County, beginning around midday on January 10th and continuing through the evening, with variable accumulations reported across the county. A trained spotter reported 3.0 inches about 1 mile south-southwest of the London-Corbin Airport. A broadcast meteorologist reported about 3.2 inches in the Sublimity City area, 2 miles south of London. The highest reported amount came from a member of the public at Lamero, with approximately 4.0 inches of snowfall.

Precipitation began as mainly snow on the morning of January 5th, before changing over to a mix of snow, sleet, freezing rain, and rain that persisted through the day on the 6th. In the early morning hours of January 6th, at 0053EST, the ASOS station at the London-Corbin Airport reported a storm total of 0.27 inches of ice accretion. Later that morning at 0800EST, the CoCoRaHS observer at station KY-LL-6 (London 4.2 S) reported a total of 1.42 inches of liquid precipitation from the wintry mix.

The ASOS weather station at the London-Corbin Airport reported a peak wind gust of 49 mph during the morning hours. However most of the reports of downed trees, up to around 20 according to Laurel County dispatch, occurred between 1100 AM EST and 300 PM EST and were most numerous in the City of London as well as Swiss Colony and Bald Rock.

While no storm total reports were made on January 16, two reports came on on the 15th which were exceeding warning criteria. At 4:30pm, an amateure radio operator reported 4.2 inches of snow so far in the community of Keavy. A little later at 6:45pm, broadcast media reported 5 inches of snow 2 miles south of the London-Corbin Airport.

recent.narrative: Snow accumulated steadily across Johnson County on January 19th. Public reports showed the snow deepening during the day, with an estimated 1.0 inch at East Point at 1100EST, followed by an estimated 2.0 inches near Whitehouse at 1400EST, and an estimated 3.0 inches near Staffordsville by 1620EST. A final storm total of a measured 4.6 inches was reported from the Paintsville 1 E CO-OP site at 700EST on January 20th.

A winter storm brought a mix of heavy snow and significant ice to Johnson County on January 5th and 6th. On the afternoon of January 5th, multiple public reports of heavy snow were received. At 1520 EST, an estimated 6 inches of snow was reported in Paintsville. At 1539 EST, a member of the public reported 5.0 inches of snow in Wittensville. Later that evening at 2200 EST, another public report noted a measurement of 5.0 inches of snow at Flat Gap. The precipitation then transitioned to freezing rain. On January 6th, a public report from Staffordsville at 1159 EST indicated approximately 0.50 inches of flat ice accretion. A final storm total of 5.5 inches of snow was reported for the entire event by a CO-OP Observer located 1 mile east of Paintsville.

The Kentucky Mesonet station 4 miles west of Paintsville reported a peak wind gust of 39 mph at 1130 AM EST. Locally higher wind gusts likely occurred given substantial siding damage inflicted on the 6th floor of the high-rise Bristlebuck Manor in the city of Paintsville.

Amounts were fairly uniform across Johnson County on the morning of January 16. A 6.0 inch report was received 1 mile E of Paintsville at 7am (this was an increase from a 4.0 report 24 hours earlier). Meanwhile, 6.5 inches was reported at 3 different sites - West Van Lear at 8:35am, Van Lear at 9:30am; and 2 miles WSW of Galen at 9:45am. A spotter report also came in the day before, on January 15 at 10:08pm, which stated that 5.5 inches of snow had fallen 1 mile NW of Auxier, near Prestonsburg, and it was still snowing at the time of the report.

High winds resulted in reports of trees down across the county. At 11:25 AM EDT, public reported multiple trees blown down near Sitka Church along Route 201. Then at 12:12 PM EDT, multiple trees and powerlines were reported to have been downed near Pickle Fork at Route 40W. A picture from the Big Sandy RECC also showed a large pine tree having fallen onto powerlines near Elna.

Other reports from later in the afternoon included 5.0 inches at Jeffersonville at 1615EST. The precipitation began to transition by late afternoon, with an NWS employee south of Oggs Station reporting that 5 inches of snow had fallen and was changing to sleet at 1630EST. On January 6th, the precipitation fell primarily as freezing rain. An NWS employee reported 0.45 inches of flat ice accretion along Spruce Valley Lane at 0630EST. recent.narrative: Flooding was reported during the afternoon on KY-130 south of Uniontown. Rainfall rates in the area peaked at around 1/hr.
Quarter size hail was estimated near Sullivan.

An EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 155 mph impacted the south side of Morganfield, KY, on the evening of May 16, 2025. The tornado began along Bunger Road where ground scouring of newly-planted crops was seen. Moving east, the tornado intensified,|doing EF-3 damage to several homes on Highway 130, Robinson Road, US Highway 60, Terre Hill Road, and Wildlife Road. Some homes suffered near catastrophic damage, with most roofs and most exterior walls removed. The tornado weakened after it crossed Highway 56 moving east, lifting near Kit Harris Road. The tornado reached a peak width of around 500 yards and caused four minor injuries along its 9.94 miles track.

Thunderstorm winds lifted the roof of a home on Highway 758 south southeast of Morganfield, causing a few columns on the porch to become displaced. Some shingles and guttering were also removed, and the HVAC system was turned on its side.
Hail to the size of quarters fell just east of Morganfield.
A cold air funnel formed between Sullivan and Pride.
